variants.reconstruction:
%n lūman lā (|) bēlu | umašširanni
#note: @bib{RN3205@280} suggests that the beginning of the line should be read @i{lūman lā} instead of @i{lū mannu}, thus introducing a conditional clause. The commentary on this line, equating @i{lūman} with @i{inanna} (courtesy of E. Jiménez), confirms this interpretation. The same equation is also found in a commentary on Neo-Babylonian grammatical texts (@akk{lu-man : i-na-an-na}; see @bib{RN2103@79 l. 16} and @bib{RN3048ff@l. 16}).

lines.translation: #tr.en: I who came back here from the grave came in through the “Gate of [Sunrise],”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ina ka-hegal | hegallu | inne[šra?]
#note: The readings @i{in}[@i{nadinanni}] (@bib{RN2721@Ḫ, 168b}), @akk{in-n[a-ad-na-an-ni]} (@bib{RN432@60}) and @akk{in-tan-[di-na-an-ni]} (@bib{RN2254@432}) do not fit into the space available at the end of the line. The signs in BabLB1 clearly are @akk{in-ne₂-[...]} (see @bib{RN90@28}), which suggests that the verb in question is I-ʾ (e-group), possibly @i{ešēru} N “to advance against/toward so.” (see @bib{RN2721@E, 363}). This would form a parallel with the verb @i{ṭehû} in the following line.
